## 6. Options Analysis

**Decision scope:** whether to add a session that accepts work from an upper orchestrator, supervises its own external sessions, and reports an aggregate result upward. This is not a decision about whether parallel work is useful, whether child worktrees may exist, or whether existing command-internal helpers should remain available.

### Evidence conventions and citation key

- **[CODE-VERIFIED—normative]** means the current instruction or approved decision was verified. It does not mean software automatically enforces it.
- **[CODE-VERIFIED—static]** means the implementation path was established by source inspection, not live execution.
- **[UNVERIFIED]** identifies an unresolved runtime fact, proposed capability, or missing measurement.
- Effort, risk and comparative ratings below are **analytical judgments**, not measured estimates. Effort covers the stated option, not all of the proposed `/sc:orchestrator`.
- **External context** supplements local evidence; it does not authorize a local policy change.

The eight numbered reports, four web reports and their complete matching returned-JSON text were read, including the full contract-by-option and launcher-reuse matrices. The scope discovery, gaps register and controlling corrections were also considered. No sibling synthesis output was used.

W04 rates the primary wording HIGH reliability, while unexecuted operational details remain qualified.

### O1 — Keep two tiers and no sub mode; clarify the PR #449 wording

**Description**

Retain the person-opened coordinator over directly supervised workers. Clarify ownership language so that “a coordinator under another orchestrator” cannot be mistaken for an existing worker exception.

**How it works**

The coordinator owns Task creation, dispatch, admission and further-work decisions. Workers can use their commands’ existing internal helpers but return newly discovered external work to the coordinator. Child worktrees remain placement decisions, not another supervisory tier. **[CODE-VERIFIED—normative]** WC:47, 60–69, 220–246.

| Assessment | Judgment |
|---|---|
| Effort | **S** for the wording/distribution correction; retaining the topology itself adds no runtime mechanism. This does not estimate the proposed v1 orchestrator. |
| Risk | **Low incremental risk.** Existing liveness and bound-supervisor probe issues remain; O1 does not certify them solved. |
| Reuse of existing code | Existing worker identity, Run/Dispatch messages, return contracts, admission rules, retries, freezes and internal helpers. |
| Files/systems affected | Section 8, O1 change-surface row: root/core ownership guidance, ccsession README, source/plugin hook message, exact-message test and distributed copies. The role/parity test may remain unchanged if its valid role assertions still hold. R07:67–76. |
| Value and unlocks | Keeps one supervision/admission boundary and permits direct parallel workers without changing depth or delegated authority. |
| Rules to rethink | WC-13 and D5 remain. PR #449 wording needs a precise ownership meaning; a separate Orca-calling slash entry point still needs a deliberate command-boundary decision. |
| Evidence | R01:62–80, 86–127; R02:123–136; R07:67–76. Source anchors: WC:5, 40, 60–69, 239–246. |
| Pros | Smallest external-supervision model; no invented upward protocol; preserves current human and Git ownership boundaries. |
| Cons | Runtime-discovered external splits still require a coordinator round trip. Internal helpers still lack separate Orca records. A permanent rejection would go beyond the available benefit evidence. |

### O2 — Independent peer coordinators opened by the person

**Description**

Use several person-opened coordinators with separately owned workstreams, rather than one coordinator supervising another.

**How it works**

Each peer owns its own Tasks, workers, result admission and authorized outward actions. Shared findings may be exchanged as evidence, but one peer does not silently claim another peer’s ready Task, consume its mailbox, approve its halt, or publish its work. This arrangement has no automatic upper/lower completion relationship. **[CODE-VERIFIED—normative]** WC:69, 200, 229–246; R01:133–146.

| Assessment | Judgment |
|---|---|
| Effort | **S** for independent peers with explicit work division. A new shared registry or cross-peer control protocol is additional, unestimated scope. |
| Risk | **Medium.** Ownership overlap, shared writes, dependency admission and duplicated intervention remain possible without clear boundaries. |
| Reuse of existing code | Existing root coordinator/worker machinery, separate Run mailboxes, durable reports and current placement rules. |
| Files/systems affected | Section 8, O2 row: routing/ownership clarification in the contract, routing-guide copies and developer guide if formalized. No inherent depth change or blanket never-as-worker change. Bound-session launch/probe policy is conditional. R07:78–88. |
| Value and unlocks | Persistent, separately owned workstreams without worker-to-supervisor conversion. Compatible with the multiple-orchestrator observation premise in #409. |
| Rules to rethink | Preserve WC-13 and D5. Define peer boundaries, not transitive supervisory authority. PR #449’s subordinate wording is not explained merely by having several peers. |
| Evidence | R01:84–105, 133–146; R02:126; R04:103–105; R07:78–88; R08:106. |
| Pros | Fits person-opened coordinator eligibility; does not need another Dispatch generation; separates persistent ownership. |
| Cons | Does not fulfill the requested “takes orders from and reports to an orchestrator above” relationship. Person-opened does not mean unbound. Cross-peer communication is not result admission or human approval. |

**External context:** Independent sessions can exchange text, but acceptance, application and completion are distinct. [Claude Code message delivery](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/cross-session-messaging#message-delivery) supports this distinction; it does not define an Orca peer-control contract. W01:44–48, 53.

### O3 — Supervised sub-orchestrator as a worker with native helpers

**Description**

A dispatched worker becomes a bounded supervisor of native Orca helpers while retaining its own parent-facing worker identity. This is the corrected, session-layer D5 option (b), not the superseded proposal to make ordinary commands dispatch workers.

**How it works**

The proposed middle session would use the existing local helper path in its own Dispatch’s Run, with individual child Task/Dispatch records. Relevant helper reports and blocking questions route to the creating Dispatch; the middle session separately reports its own outcome upward. A depth-two policy would require a defined composite brief, explicit WC-13 exception and bounds. None of those permissions follows from source capability. R03:62–81; R06:114–128.

```text
Person-opened coordinator
          |
     middle Dispatch
       /       \
 child Dispatch child Dispatch
```

The diagram describes the candidate relationship, not an approved or live-verified topology.

| Assessment | Judgment |
|---|---|
| Effort | **XL** for a complete authorized mode: role/brief semantics, dual supervision, aggregate outcomes, enforcement, recovery and deployment evidence. Existing transport reduces invention, not those obligations. |
| Risk | **High.** A stalled or compromised middle session affects both its upper assignment and live descendants. |
| Reuse of existing code | Strongest native supervised fit: helper ancestry, same-Run scope, creator-directed reports/questions, generation fencing and selected-mail hand-back. Existing flat admission and retry rules are reusable constraints, not a completed recursive contract. |
| Files/systems affected | Section 8, O3 row: WC role/brief/report/retry/admission/placement rules; contract tests; routing guides; ownership guidance; governed launch/report/probe policy where applicable; decision amendment and distributed copies. WC-8 can remain if fan-out stays outside commands. R07:90–102. |
| Value and unlocks | Potentially avoids an upper-coordinator wake/read/Task-creation round trip for a genuinely unforeseen split while retaining Orca tracking for children. Saving is **[UNVERIFIED]**, not measured. |
| Rules to rethink | Explicitly reopen WC-13, coordinator eligibility and D5. Define bounded planning authority, helper count, question/retry budgets, result reduction and root-retained outward authority. Preserve D1’s explicit mode, D2 human Rulings and D3 PR placement. |
| Evidence | R01:86–148; R02:85–132; R03:43–81, 133–164; R06:75–82, 114–142; R07:90–102. |
| Pros | Native parent/child provenance and upward routing already exist in inspected code. More direct fit than creating a second ordinary-owner protocol. |
| Cons | Currently prohibited. Composite authority, mixed-mail handling, aggregate admission, blocked-parent service, replacement ownership, effective settings and safe lowering are unresolved. Local helpers are same-host/new-agent on the inspected route; remote behavior is separate. |

**External context:** Public Orca requests support the usefulness of local reviewers/helpers, but provide no measured IronClaude saving. [Local delegation request](https://github.com/stablyai/orca/issues/24970), [remote request](https://github.com/stablyai/orca/issues/30141). W04:37–41 rates demand evidence MEDIUM reliability; it does not satisfy D5.

### O4 — Handoff-owner sub-orchestrator through ordinary launches and a new upward protocol

**Description**

Launch a non-dispatched owner session using the existing ordinary agent/worktree launch mechanisms, then give it a separately defined upper-assignment and reporting relationship.

**How it works**

Ordinary launch creates an agent surface and receipt, not automatic Run/Task/Dispatch records or a worker preamble. The launched owner could only become a recognized subordinate coordinator through a new eligibility and authority contract. Its upward protocol must define correlation, progress, questions, application acknowledgments, completion, admission and failure handling. A new transport or message type is not necessarily required. R03:83–116; R02:128–132.

| Assessment | Judgment |
|---|---|
| Effort | **XL.** Launch mechanics exist, but the missing upward lifecycle and owner-authority contract are central rather than incidental work. |
| Risk | **High.** Ordinary-launch freedom can conceal missing supervision, stale ownership or excessive authority if treated as equivalent to a Dispatch. |
| Reuse of existing code | Agent/worktree launch, launch receipts, watcher durable intent/audit and artifact returns. These are partial components, not a complete subordinate-owner protocol. |
| Files/systems affected | Section 8, O4 row: role eligibility, ordinary upward reporting, ownership/outward boundaries, routing guides, ownership copies/tests and applicable governed-session policy. New command eligibility is a separate conditional surface. R07:104–115. |
| Value and unlocks | Could support persistent domain ownership outside the worker lifecycle without needing another Dispatch generation on the ordinary launch itself. |
| Rules to rethink | Person-opened coordinator eligibility, ordinary-owner reporting and authority division. WC-13 still prohibits a worker from initiating this route. D5’s numeric raise trigger is not a substitute for the separate O4 authority decision. |
| Evidence | R01:53–58, 129–148; R02:128–132; R03:83–116; R05:40–75; R07:104–115; R08:117–125. |
| Pros | Reuses real ordinary-launch mechanisms; separates a persistent workstream owner from a one-Task worker. |
| Cons | Does not inherit worker lifecycle guarantees, coordinator eligibility, grant rights or human authority. Guide handoff-owner behavior is not a monitored subordinate supervisor. More protocol invention than O3. |

The phrase “new upward channel” therefore means **a new agreed reporting relationship**, not a finding that no generic transport exists. Worktree lineage has host/instance validation, but is not that relationship. R03:85–100.

### O5 — In-session sub-orchestration through existing Agent-tool helpers

**Description**

Keep decomposition inside the dispatched command/session using its already permitted internal helpers.

**How it works**

The worker invokes the assigned command at top level. That command may use its own helpers and collect their findings. Nested command contracts propagate according to the existing rules; only the top-level worker sends Orca lifecycle messages and completion. Wrapping the whole assigned command in a helper is excluded by WC-7. **[CODE-VERIFIED—normative]** WC:24–25, 46, 60.

| Assessment | Judgment |
|---|---|
| Effort | **XS** to use an already supported helper pattern. A new generic wrapper or changed protocol is not included or proposed here. |
| Risk | **Medium**, principally context loss, output fidelity and helper behavior; less new operational authority than O3/O4. |
| Reuse of existing code | Existing command-to-skill activation, helper dispatch/collection and nested-result propagation; strongest direct specialist-helper precedent in the launcher inventory. |
| Files/systems affected | Section 8, O5 row: no policy change inherent in selecting existing helpers. New wrappers would conditionally affect command declarations, unattended expectations and nested behavior. Ownership clarification is separate. R07:117–126. |
| Value and unlocks | Parallel, bounded investigation/review with less parent-context clutter, without a second external supervision relationship. |
| Rules to rethink | No WC-13 or D5 reversal for existing internal fan-out. Retain top-level Skill invocation, lifecycle ownership, nested failure propagation and human-only boundaries. |
| Evidence | R01:77, 93–101; R02:129; R03:163; R05:44–61, 71–75; R07:117–126. |
| Pros | Existing narrow mechanism; no new Run/Task/Dispatch ownership or ordinary upward protocol. Local/background Agent classification does not itself receive ESCAPE. |
| Cons | Does not deliver independently supervised Orca children, child lifecycle/retry records or persistent external owners. Accepted heartbeat gaps remain. No universal absence of provider/adapter limits has been proved. |

**External context:** Current provider documentation supports bounded subagent nesting; it does not prove this installed harness’s behavior or authorize Orca worker fan-out. [Subagents](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/sub-agents). Fresh context also incurs briefing/reconstruction costs; it is not automatically cheaper or faster. W01:48; W02, Findings 5–6.

### O6 — Defer a new sub mode with explicit reconsideration gates

**Description**

Do not add or authorize `--sub` on the present evidence. Keep the current operating boundary and make the missing evidence and authority decisions explicit.

**How it works**

Existing flat supervision and permitted internal helpers remain available under their current rules. A later hierarchy decision must pass the applicable gates in Section 7.5; satisfying a mechanism gate does not itself approve a policy change. This is bounded deferral, not permanent rejection or authorization to build another part of the system.

| Assessment | Judgment |
|---|---|
| Effort | **S** for the decision and gate record. The effort of satisfying later gates is not hidden inside that rating or scheduled here. |
| Risk | **Low incremental risk.** The cost is delayed access to a benefit whose local magnitude has not been established. Existing operational gaps remain visible. |
| Reuse of existing code | Current operating model, existing internal helpers, current static helper findings and WC:246’s follow-up/time evidence channel. |
| Files/systems affected | Section 8, O6 row: decision/gate documentation only; no nested runtime or guard relaxation inherent. Ownership-wording correction, if separately adopted, has O1’s surface. R07:128–145. |
| Value and unlocks | Keeps a credible O3 candidate open while preventing an undefined role from acquiring launch, approval, publication or cleanup authority by name. |
| Rules to rethink | None are silently changed. D5’s two-part trigger, SPEC/REC mailbox discrepancy, command packaging and any future WC-13 exception remain explicit decisions. |
| Evidence | R01:113–148; R03:152–164; R06:54–82, 130–142; R07:128–145; R08:127–133; GQ:G02–G19, G27–G35. |
| Pros | Matches the current authority boundary and the present evidence gap; reversible; distinguishes static feasibility from operational readiness. |
| Cons | Does not deliver a subordinate external supervisor now. It needs concrete evidence to avoid becoming an indefinite, untestable “later.” |

### Options Comparison

Ratings compare the stated options, not a fully implemented v1 product. “Existing” means source/instructions exist; it does not mean live compliance has been demonstrated.

| Criterion | O1 Two tiers | O2 Person-opened peers | O3 Supervised helpers | O4 Launched owner | O5 Internal helpers | O6 Gated deferral |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Effort | S | S for independent peers | XL | XL | XS for existing use | S for decision record |
| Risk | Low incremental; existing gaps remain | Medium ownership overlap | High dual-role/recovery | High new lifecycle/authority | Medium output/context risk | Low incremental; opportunity cost |
| Maintainability | Fewest supervisory relationships | Existing mechanisms, more ownership boundaries | Native machinery helps; recursive contract broadens | Separate owner/reporting contract adds maintenance | Existing protocols; no external tier | No new runtime behavior; gates must stay evidence-based |
| Integration complexity | Low topology change | Low independently; higher if shared control is demanded | High across policy, mail, admission, recovery and guards | High across eligibility, reporting, monitoring and grants | Low within supported command patterns | Low now |
| Reuse potential | High current model | High current root machinery | High native ancestry/routing reuse | Partial launch/audit/result reuse | High existing helper patterns | High existing policy/evidence channels |
| Liveness and reporting fit | Existing single-edge procedure; not proven automatic | Separate loops, no automatic upward completion | Best native nested fit; aggregate/blocked-parent/recovery open | No equivalent upward lifecycle established | Parent result only; no child Orca lifecycle | Preserves current fit and exposes unresolved cases |
| Authority-model fit | Fits current policy | Fits if genuinely independent | Direct WC-13/eligibility conflict | New eligibility/authority case; not worker bypass | Fits existing WC-7 boundary | Fits current policy without declaring it permanent |
| Enforceability by hooks or Orca | Partial; B1/B2 remain | Same qualification when bound | Depth/identity machinery exists; scoped authority not enforced by current hooks | Ordinary launch is not Dispatch authority; current hooks lack role scope | Local Agent branch compatible; actual identity inheritance unverified | No new enforcement claimed |
| Value delivered | Direct supervision and parallel workers | Persistent independent owners | Conditional local autonomy plus tracked children | Conditional persistent delegated ownership | Local specialist decomposition | Evidence-based, reversible decision; no new hierarchy |

**Comparison conclusion:** O3 is the strongest technical candidate **if** a subordinate supervised role becomes justified. It is not ready merely because native helper transport exists. O4 has weaker lifecycle reuse, O2 is not hierarchical, and O5 is not independent external supervision. O6 is the supported present decision because the remaining failures concern authority, demonstrated need and recovery—not an obsolete claim that nesting is technically impossible.

### Clause-by-option compatibility and preservation

The complete clause matrix in R01’s returned JSON, §§5.2–5.7, is retained as the detailed assessment. The matrix below carries its load-bearing distinctions into this decision without reproducing lengthy quotations.

**H:** compatible requirement retained, not live-tested.  
**B:** defining behavior conflicts with the current rule.  
**U:** necessary cross-level ownership or behavior is undefined.  
**C:** conditional on a stated restriction.  
For O4, an H on worker protections does **not** promote the ordinary launched owner to an eligible coordinator.

## 7. Recommendation

**Recommended approach: Option O6 — defer a new sub-orchestrator mode with explicit reconsideration gates.**

This recommendation retains the existing operating contract; it does not permanently select O1 against all future hierarchy. Native supervised helpers, O3, are the strongest candidate for a later positive decision because current source supplies real ancestry and creator-directed routing. The present evidence does not establish the additional authority, measured need and full lifecycle contract necessary to approve that role.

### Rationale

The Options Comparison favors O6 on **current authority-model fit, incremental risk and integration burden**. O3 leads O4 on native liveness/reporting reuse, but neither has the missing operational and policy conditions established. No external benchmark supplies the local incremental benefit needed to resolve that deficit.

| Alternative | Why it is not the recommended answer to this decision |
|---|---|
| O1 | Appropriate operating baseline, but “no sub mode” as a permanent conclusion is stronger than the evidence. Native routing and public demand make bounded reconsideration credible. |
| O2 | Useful for independent persistent owners, but not the requested supervised upper/lower relationship. It does not solve aggregate upward completion. |
| O3 | Best future technical candidate, but presently conflicts with WC-13/eligibility and lacks a defined autonomous brief, qualifying measured need, aggregate admission and verified recovery. |
| O4 | Uses a different ownership model with less ready-made upward lifecycle support. Avoiding a Dispatch-depth check is not equivalent to authorized supervised delegation. |
| O5 | Useful existing local decomposition, but does not supply independently supervised Orca sessions, per-child lifecycle or persistent external ownership. |

This conclusion does **not** depend on the disproved premises that helper reports always go to the root, that commands can carry only one line, that D1 bans all other flags, or that all executable spellings are mechanically blocked. It depends on the surviving evidence in R01’s full rule matrix, R02’s dual-role state/ack analysis, R03’s current mechanics, R04’s corrections, R06’s trigger investigation and R08’s authority requirements.

### 7.1 Value

| Value question | Finding |
|---|---|
| What unique benefit could justify O3? | Local supervision of a coherent split discovered during execution, with independently tracked child records, potentially avoiding an upper coordinator wake/read/Task-creation round trip. R06:116–126; R03:62–81. |
| What is already obtainable without it? | Direct parallel workers, existing flat fan-in, internal specialist helpers and separately owned person-opened workstreams. R01:86–125; R05:40–75. |
| Has the incremental saving been demonstrated? | **[UNVERIFIED]** No qualifying combined record of runtime-only discovery and material added coordination time was found in the bounded search. This is not proof no such record exists elsewhere. R06:79–96. |
| What value does deferral deliver? | Prevents authority from being granted through ambiguous wording, preserves a better-supported native candidate, and turns “not ready” into falsifiable conditions rather than a permanent ban. |
| What must not count as value evidence? | Long command duration, heartbeat gaps, follow-up work alone, larger worker counts, public feature availability or vendor multi-agent-versus-single-agent metrics. None isolates the proposed middle layer’s benefit. |

**External context:** Task-shape guidance supports dynamic decomposition when subtasks cannot reasonably be specified beforehand, not merely when a task is large. [Building effective agents](https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/building-effective-agents). Its reliability is HIGH as official guidance; transfer to this repository is an inference, not a benchmark.

### 7.2 Implications

| Area | Decision implication |
|---|---|
| Role and authority | Define a middle session’s allowed decisions, parent, children and resource scope. Worktree ownership, Dispatch identity and permission to supervise are different. |
| Upward reporting | Credit the existing native local creator route. Define application handling and aggregate admission; do not invent a new transport as a prerequisite without need. |
| Liveness | A middle session owes its own parent progress and its children supervision. Child heartbeats, mailbox traffic or a monitoring transcript cannot substitute for its own semantic progress. |
| Blocking and failure | An upstream `ask`, permission prompt, fencing, context exhaustion or exit must leave a known owner for live children. Selected-mail hand-back is not complete supervisory takeover. |
| Evidence and completion | Keep send, receive, apply, command result, Task settlement, admitted aggregate and safe cleanup separate. No ancestor synthesizes another worker’s completion. |
| Retry and resources | Helper count, attempts, questions, costly probes and recovery budgets need lineage-wide accounting. Replacing a supervisor must not reset allowances or redo completed work. |
| Human authority | A parent agent’s message, credential or accepted inbound text is not a human Ruling, fresh Task-specific commit instruction, publication approval or permission-setting change. |
| Governed sessions | Literal executable recognition, launch/report permissions and required read probes need explicit treatment. B1 is an enforcement ceiling; B2 is a compatibility gap. Neither grants a bypass or mandates an allowlist expansion. |
| Version and settings | Source default, stored profile, effective runtime value and public release behavior must be recorded separately. A newer public migration may broaden capability without changing local policy. |
| Distribution | Source, project development copies, plugin mirrors, installed core files and packaged assets have different update paths. A sync or build alone does not establish universal installed freshness. R07:141–145. |

**External context:** OTP illustrates multiplied retry budgets and the distinction between stopping a parent and stopping descendants; it does not prove an OTP-style defect exists locally. [Supervisor principles](https://www.erlang.org/doc/system/sup_princ.html). Claude-native messaging likewise cannot supply human consent or route around sender restrictions. [Incoming-message boundaries](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/cross-session-messaging#how-a-session-treats-an-incoming-message).

**Gate interpretation**

- DG-01 and DG-02 preserve D5’s **two-part revisit trigger**.
- DG-06 acknowledges both the historical trace and the stronger current source findings; it does not require pretending those findings are absent.
- DG-08 separates **static routing established** from **live operation unverified**.
- DG-15 and DG-16 are not satisfiable by another agent’s report claiming the user approved something.
- DG-18 through DG-21 reflect the typed-message/grant conditions in #339 without selecting a token library or treating every transport as identical.
- Applicability exclusions must name the omitted capability. Excluding remote helpers, for example, cannot support a claim of remote helper readiness.

### 7.6 What would change this recommendation

| New evidence or decision | Effect on the recommendation |
|---|---|
| D5’s composite brief is explicitly defined and a qualifying material runtime-only split record is produced | Removes the principal need/brief barriers to reconsidering O3; does not by itself settle authority or recovery. |
| The applicable authority, lifecycle, enforcement and human-boundary gates pass for native local helpers | Supports changing from O6 to **O3 for that bounded, evidenced scope**, not unrestricted recursion. |
| A real persistent-owner use case is demonstrated that native Dispatch helpers cannot adequately serve, and O4’s separate eligibility/upward lifecycle gates pass | Could justify O4 as a distinct ownership mode rather than a depth workaround. |
| Work is shown to need only self-contained investigation/review, not independent session lifecycle | Resolves that use case with existing O5; it does not justify an external `--sub` mode. |
| Work is shown to require independent persistent owners but no upper/lower supervision | Favors O2 for that use case, without claiming hierarchy. |
| Measurements show extra manager planning, context transfer, reconciliation or recovery outweighs saved coordinator work | Strengthens O1 as the enduring topology for that workload rather than merely deferring. |
| A runtime upgrade changes default depth, migration or shutdown behavior | Requires re-evaluation of the affected capability gates. It is not approval to change IronClaude’s authority policy. |
| A gate cannot be met without weakening person-only decisions, protected-worktree checks or bounded recovery | Keeps O6, or supports rejecting that variant. Convenience does not justify transitive human approval. |
